extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and professionals interested in science, higher education, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and normative statements about the proper relation between science and religion in universities, how to measure civilization by scientific contributions, and how philanthropy and institutional governance should support scientific inquiry. Includes criteria for who should decide scientific questions and what counts as appropriate support for research and researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best criterion of a nation's civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The best criterion of the position which a nation has gained in the scale of civilization is the contributions which its men of thought have made toward the understanding and the conquest of Nature, and the popular and public appreciation that has been reached regarding this kind of intellectual labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a test of national advancement; contrasted with other proposed measures (arts, religion, literature, government, diffusion of education). Implies measuring civilization by scientific output and public esteem for science rather than solely by material or artistic accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific questions must be decided by scientific evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigation [e.g., of the antiquity of man] belongs entirely to science, and must be pursued and determined on the basis of scientific evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against theological or purely grammatical/Biblical methods of settling empirical questions. Example: Prof. Winchell's treatment of man’s antiquity is scientific and not antagonistic to religion; dismissal for holding such views is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science's mission: pursue truth without compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Science will not cease to advance with its work, come what may... It cannot pause, it cannot compromise. Its business is the study of Nature; its object to find out the utmost truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames an evaluative standard for institutional behavior: universities and trustees should not ask science to halt or temper its inquiries. Implies that institutional constraints that force compromise are failures of governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities should not muzzle independent teachers of scientific truth
rubrics_metrics.description: An educational body that uses its power to muzzle, repress, silence, and discredit independent teachers of scientific truth is acting contrary to the interests of science and civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct criticism of Vanderbilt University's dismissal of a professor for his scientific views; used as a governance criterion for academic freedom and institutional responsibility to support, not punish, scientific inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philanthropy ought to support science and research training
rubrics_metrics.description: When the results of scientific work have ripened to acquisitions of wealth, some portion of it, at least, should be devoted to the advancement of the interests of science; benefactions should be directed to encouragement and promotion of scientific investigation and training of researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues moral obligation of wealthy donors (e.g., Vanderbilt) to fund science rather than exclusively sectarian ends. Cites the scarcity of funds for scientific societies and for funds like the Tyndall fund as evidence of neglect; suggests donors should prioritize research training and institutions of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing utilitarian, wealth-yielding studies is a negative indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of the utilitarian spirit, which is gradually substituting immediate, practical, wealth-yielding studies for the more elevated, disinterested, and ennobling intellectual pursuits, is a decline of interest that threatens perversion and degradation of civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels 'Americanization' where material utilities are privileged over disinterested science; use as a cultural metric to evaluate priorities in education, philanthropy, and public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/regional appreciation of scientists as a metric
rubrics_metrics.description: How does the community regard a man who gives his life to investigation — are they held in high honor, encouraged, or treated with indifference, neglect, or contempt? That degree of intellectual appreciation indicates national priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as a measure for social esteem of scientific labor; illustrated by comparison between English example (Cavendish honored by devotion) and typical American attitudes (materialist contempt), and used to evaluate whether a society properly supports scientific work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of professorial or institutional appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Trustees and faculties of institutions (especially those endowed by wealth created by science/industry) should shape university policy in harmony with the progress of science and not use endowments to hinder or crush scientific thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of universities founded with industrial wealth but run on sectarian/antiscientific lines; implies criterion that institutional appointments, dismissals, and curricula should foster scientific inquiry rather than enforce theological conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donations/funds should target training capable researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts for science (e.g., the Tyndall fund) should be used to assist in promoting the education of young men who possess talent for physical researches and wish to qualify themselves for pursuing the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for philanthropic impact: priority to training and enabling researchers over creating merely named chairs, buildings, or superficial endowments. Evidence: Tyndall fund's limited size and lack of additional contributions shows neglect.
